# Angiotensin Receptor-Neprilysin Inhibition in Heart Failure: A Narrative Review

### Introduction and Pharmacological Rationale
Heart failure (HF) remains a major global health burden associated with high morbidity, mortality, and healthcare expenditures. The pathophysiological hallmark of HF involves chronic neurohormonal overactivation, characterized by sustained activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) and the sympathetic nervous system. Historically, therapeutic strategies focused exclusively on blocking these harmful pathways. However, a modern paradigm shift aims to simultaneously augment the adaptive, cardioprotective natriuretic peptide system.

Angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibition (ARNI) represents a first-in-class therapeutic class designed to achieve this dual neurohormonal modulation [1]. Sacubitril/valsartan consists of the neprilysin inhibitor prodrug sacubitril and the angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB) valsartan [2]. Neprilysin is a zinc metallopeptidase responsible for degrading various endogenous vasoactive peptides, including atrial, B-type, and C-type natriuretic peptides, bradykinin, and adrenomedullin [1]. Inhibiting neprilysin preserves these peptides, promoting vasodilation, natriuresis, diuresis, and the inhibition of hypertrophy and fibrosis [2]. However, neprilysin also degrades angiotensin II. Consequently, isolated neprilysin inhibition leads to an accumulation of angiotensin II, necessitating the concomitant blockade of the angiotensin II type 1 (AT1) receptor [2]. Combining neprilysin inhibition with an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor is contraindicated due to an unacceptably high risk of life-threatening angioedema caused by redundant bradykinin degradation pathways; thus, sacubitril is paired specifically with the ARB valsartan.

### Clinical Evidence in Heart Failure with Reduced Ejection Fraction (HFrEF)
The landmark PARADIGM-HF phase III trial established sacubitril/valsartan as a cornerstone of HFrEF therapy [3]. Comparing sacubitril/valsartan with the ACE inhibitor enalapril in 8,442 patients with chronic HFrEF (LVEF ≤ 40%, later amended to ≤ 35%), the trial was stopped early due to overwhelming evidence of clinical benefit [3]. Sacubitril/valsartan demonstrated a 20% relative risk reduction in the primary composite endpoint of cardiovascular death or HF hospitalization [3]. Furthermore, ARNI therapy slowed overall clinical progression, decreased the need for intensive care, and reduced the requirement for intravenous inotropic support [4].

Subsequent research shifted focus to the acute decompensated setting. The PIONEER-HF trial evaluated the in-hospital initiation of sacubitril/valsartan in patients admitted with acute decompensated HF (ADHF) after achieving hemodynamic stability [5]. Over an 8-week period, patients randomized to sacubitril/valsartan experienced a significantly greater reduction in N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) compared with those receiving enalapril [5]. Critically, exploratory analyses from PIONEER-HF revealed a significant reduction in serious clinical events, such as rehospitalization and death, supporting early in-hospital initiation [6]. These findings were supported by the TRANSITION trial, which showed that initiating sacubitril/valsartan either in the hospital or shortly after discharge was safe, well-tolerated, and resulted in comparable therapeutic adherence [7].

The structural benefits of sacubitril/valsartan were explored in the PROVE-HF trial, which demonstrated a strong association between the reduction of NT-proBNP and significant reverse cardiac remodeling, including improvements in left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) and decreases in left ventricular volumes [8]. In parallel, the EVALUATE-HF trial showed that sacubitril/valsartan led to favorable changes in central aortic stiffness and ventricular-arterial coupling compared to enalapril, providing a mechanistic basis for its clinical efficacy [9].

### Expanding the Spectrum: HFmrEF and HFpEF
Given its success in HFrEF, ARNI was investigated in patients with preserved and mildly reduced ejection fractions. The Phase II PARAMOUNT trial first demonstrated that sacubitril/valsartan significantly reduced NT-proBNP levels in patients with HFpEF (LVEF ≥ 45%) compared to valsartan alone at 12 weeks [10]. This paved the way for the Phase III PARAGON-HF trial, which randomized 4,822 patients with HFpEF (LVEF ≥ 45%) to receive sacubitril/valsartan or valsartan [11]. While ARNI achieved a 13% reduction in the primary composite endpoint of total HF hospitalizations and cardiovascular death, this narrowly missed statistical significance [11]. However, prespecified subgroup analyses revealed significant heterogeneous treatment benefits, particularly in patients with LVEF on the lower end of the spectrum (45–57%) and in women [11].

To clarify these findings, a pooled participant-level analysis of both PARADIGM-HF and PARAGON-HF was conducted [12]. The analysis demonstrated that the treatment benefit of sacubitril/valsartan on cardiovascular death and HF hospitalizations extends across a broad spectrum of ejection fractions, with therapeutic efficacy persisting up to an LVEF of approximately 55–60% [12]. This encompasses the category of heart failure with mildly reduced ejection fraction (HFmrEF). The PARALLAX trial further confirmed that sacubitril/valsartan significantly reduced NT-proBNP compared with individualized medical therapy in HFpEF, although it did not show a significant improvement in 6-minute walk distance [13].

### Special Populations, Safety, and Clinical Practice Recommendations
The clinical utility of sacubitril/valsartan has been explored in diverse clinical settings. In the PARADISE-MI trial, sacubitril/valsartan was evaluated in patients with acute myocardial infarction without prior chronic HF, comparing it to ramipril; although it did not significantly reduce the primary composite endpoint, it demonstrated excellent safety and tolerability [14]. In patients with chronic kidney disease, the UK HARP-III trial showed that sacubitril/valsartan was well-tolerated and preserved renal function comparably to irbesartan while providing superior blood pressure control [15]. 

Further clinical analyses have established additional benefits. Sacubitril/valsartan significantly reduces the risk of sudden cardiac death and ventricular arrhythmias in HFrEF [16]. It also improves glycemic control in diabetic patients with HF, slowing the initiation of insulin therapy [17], and protects renal function by reducing the rate of decline in the estimated glomerular filtration rate compared with ACE inhibition [18]. The efficacy of sacubitril/valsartan remains consistent across the spectrum of ejection fractions [19], age [20], and background therapies [21]. Titrating to the target dose of 97/103 mg twice daily is associated with optimal long-term clinical outcomes [22]. Although neprilysin helps degrade amyloid-beta, the prospective PERSPECTIVE trial confirmed that sacubitril/valsartan does not adversely affect cognitive function or increase amyloid deposition over a 3-year period [23]. When monitoring patients, clinicians must recognize that while NT-proBNP levels decrease with effective ARNI therapy, tracking clinical recovery [24], circulating BNP levels paradoxically increase because BNP is a substrate for neprilysin [24]. Therapy also favorably modulates biomarkers of extracellular matrix turnover and fibrosis [25].

Reflecting this evidence, the 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA guidelines recommend ARNI as a Class 1 first-line therapy to reduce morbidity and mortality in HFrEF [26]. The European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guidelines similarly support its use as a core component of guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) [27,28]. Despite robust recommendations, real-world data from the CHAMP-HF registry reveal significant implementation gaps, highlighting the underutilization of sacubitril/valsartan [29]. Addressing these gaps remains a public health priority, as health economics analyses consistently demonstrate that ARNI is highly cost-effective [30].
